nodes.question: What are the main products generated from the pyrolysis of faecal sludge?
nodes.answer: The main products from the pyrolysis of faecal sludge include biochar, bio-oil, tar, and syngas.
nodes.paragraph: 1.). Recent research has investigated the thermochemical treatment by pyrol- ysis as a reliable method of treating faecal sludge. Pyrolysis involves heating biomass to temperatures of 350 1000 C in the absence of oxygen (European Biochar Foundation, 2016) which thoroughly destroys pathogenic organisms within faecal sludge (Liu et al., 2014b). This process creates a carbon-rich product, biochar, which unlike charcoal does not easily burn and the predominant use of biochar is as a soil amendment (Crombie et al., 2013). Physico-chemical properties of biochar are related to the composition of Fig. 1 Simplified overview of faecal sludge management with faecal sludge biochar as the end product 5895 Faecal sludge pyrolysis as a circular economic approach to waste the original feedstock and the pyrolysis parameters such as holding time and the highest treatment temperature (HTT) (Cairns et al., 2022). This process also yields other by- products including bio-oil, tar and syngas. The use of biochar to increase soil fertility and crop yield was introduced as a theory from observations made on Amazonian Black Earth (terra preta).

nodes.question: Why has there been a recent lack of energy-rich feedstocks for biogas production in Europe?
nodes.answer: The recent expansion of biogas production across Europe has resulted in a lack of energy-rich feedstocks such as slaughterhouse waste.

The upgrading to transport fuel offers an envi- ronmentally favorable alternative compared to com- bustion in CHP units (Styles et al. 2016). Nutrients in the organic input material are mostly retained in the residue after digestion, the digestate, which can be used as a bio-based fertilizer to recycle nutrients back to agricultural fields. The recent expansion of biogas production across Europe (Gustafsson & Anderberg 2022) has resulted in a lack of energy-rich feedstocks such as slaughterhouse waste. Potential supple- mentary feedstocks for biogas production which are receiving growing interest are cover crops (Feng et al. 2020). Cover crops are grown to reduce leaching of nutri- ents and soil erosion when there is no main crop in the field, i.e. in the time between main crops, mostly dur - ing autumn and winter.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Biomass energy|Biogas production from biomass_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the two modelled scenarios for biogas production discussed in the study?
nodes.answer: The two scenarios are (1) harvesting and ensiling of cover crops and cereal straw with co-digestion of cattle manure, and (2) mono-digestion of cattle manure with direct cover crop soil incorporation.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Cover crops offer a potential biogas feedstock, and to enable continuous operation of the biogas plant, ensiling can be used for biomass pres- ervation. The aim of the present study was to assess the environmental impacts of biogas production at an organic dairy farm for two modelled scenarios: (1) harvesting and ensiling of cover crops and cereal straw and co-digestion with cattle manure, or (2) mono-digestion of cattle manure and direct cover crop soil incorporation. The biogas scenarios were mod- elled in a consequential LCA in relation to a common baseline without anaerobic digestion, with cover crop soil incorporation and field application of raw cattle manure. Biogas scenarios resulted in decreased global warming impacts of (1) 250 and (2) 120 Mg CO2eq for a 1000-hectare example dairy farm due to substi- tution of natural gas. However, emissions from ensil- ing, biogas plant operation, and agronomic effects increased other environmental impacts. nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Biomass energy|Biogas production from biomass_qna_003
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What are some potential adverse effects associated with the use of energy crops in biogas production?
nodes.answer: Potential adverse effects include changes in land use and soil carbon storage, as well as increased energy inputs for harvesting, transport, and processing.
nodes.paragraph: Due to the widespread use of cover crops, including legumes, in organic farming, an organic dairy farm was chosen for a case study in the present study. Aside from the clear benefits with increased biogas production, the use of energy crops in biogas production may also have adverse effects related to changes in land use and soil carbon storage, as well as increased energy inputs for harvesting, transport and processing (Hamelin et al. 2014). These effects vary depending on the feedstock and case-specific factors (Hamelin et al. 2014; Hijazi et al. 2016) and the overall environmental consequences of such com- bined effects are insufficiently understood in the case of cover crop harvesting and co-digestion. Therefore, it is essential to assess the total environmental impact of the system to ensure that the use of cover crop in anaerobic digestion leads to reduced environmental impacts, for which life cycle assessment (LCA) is a suitable method. The objective of this study was to provide a com- prehensive assessment of the environmental impacts of biogas production at organic dairy farms, focus- ing on the co-digestion of cattle manure with silage of cover crops and straw.
